q: The fundamental economic problem of scarcity arises because
options: Resources are unlimited but their prices rise continuously
Government intervention restricts the free allocation of goods and services
Human wants are unlimited while the means of satisfying them are limited
Human wants are finite while the means of production are infinite
explanation: Scarcity exists because human wants are unlimited whereas the resources and time available to satisfy them are limited and have alternative uses, so rationing such as foodgrain ration cards becomes necessary.

q: In a market economy, the price mechanism performs the function of
options: Coordinating the allocation of scarce resources across competing uses
Eliminating the need for government intervention in all markets
Guaranteeing a minimum level of consumption for every household
Distributing income equitably among all sections of society
explanation: Prices act as signals and incentives: the equilibrium price equates marginal benefit with marginal cost, thereby channelling scarce resources to their most valued uses.

q: The opportunity cost of producing one more unit of a good is
options: The average cost of production of all units produced
The value of the next best alternative that has been forgone
The fixed cost of the firm divided by the number of units produced
The total money spent on producing the extra unit
explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up when a choice is made, so it measures the real cost of the extra unit in terms of what could have been produced instead.

q: Marginal utility refers to
options: Total satisfaction obtained from consuming a given quantity of a good
The satisfaction obtained from the very first unit of a good consumed
The maximum satisfaction obtainable from a bundle of goods
The additional satisfaction derived from consuming one more unit of a good
explanation: Marginal utility is the extra utility from the last unit consumed, while total utility is the sum of marginal utilities of all units, which is why the law of diminishing marginal utility applies.

q: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that
options: Marginal utility is the same for every unit of every good
Marginal utility turns negative only after total utility has started falling
As consumption of a good rises, the marginal utility from each additional unit declines
Total utility from a good always rises at an increasing rate
explanation: Diminishing marginal utility means that each successive unit of a good yields less extra satisfaction than the previous one, which is the basis of the law of demand and consumer equilibrium analysis.

q: A market characterised by very large numbers of buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, perfect information and free entry is
options: A monopolistically competitive market
A perfectly competitive market
A monopoly market
An oligopolistic market
explanation: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, identical products, free entry and exit and full information, so no single participant can influence price; the other structures involve market power.

q: A monopolist can raise prices without losing all its customers mainly because
options: The demand for its product is perfectly elastic
The government fixes its maximum price at a high level
Its product is always of superior quality to that of rivals
Barriers to entry prevent new firms from competing with it
explanation: A monopoly retains the power to influence price because entry barriers such as licences, patents, control over raw materials or scale economies keep competitors out of the market.

q: Gross Domestic Product is valued at
options: Market prices
Wholesale prices
Basic prices
Factor cost
explanation: In the Indian national accounts, GDP is published at market prices, which is gross value added at basic prices plus net taxes on products, whereas basic prices and factor cost exclude such taxes.

q: The difference between India's GDP and GNP, computed on the same basis, arises from
options: The net factor income earned by residents from abroad
The value of exports of goods and services
The depreciation of capital assets in the economy
The net unrecorded cash transactions in the economy
explanation: GNP equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad, so the two differ because of the income Indian residents earn overseas less the income earned by foreign residents in India.

q: Which of the following is NOT included in the computation of Gross Value Added at basic prices?
options: Compensation of employees
Operating surplus
Consumption of fixed capital
Net taxes on products
explanation: Gross value added at basic prices is output less intermediate consumption, and net taxes on products are added separately when converting GVA into GDP at market prices.

q: The base year used for compiling the National Accounts Statistics of India is
explanation: The Central Statistics Office uses 2011-12 as the base year for the constant price series of national accounts published since the 2019 base year revision, replacing the earlier 2004-05 base.

q: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP
options: Is calculated using current year prices
Excludes the depreciation of capital assets
Is computed at constant prices and thus removes the effect of price changes
Includes net factor income from abroad
explanation: Real GDP is expressed at base year prices so that it measures only the change in the volume of output, while nominal GDP is at current prices and mixes volume with price changes.

q: Per capita income in India is calculated as
options: Total national income divided by the labour force
Total national income divided by the working age population
Total national income divided by the mid-year total population
Total national income divided by the number of households
explanation: Per capita income is the average income of the population, obtained by dividing national income by the mid-year population, which is why a rising population dilutes per capita gains.

q: The Human Development Index is a composite of
options: Employment rate, wages and labour productivity
Life expectancy at birth, education measured by mean and expected years of schooling, and GNI per capita
Per capita income, poverty ratio and literacy rate
Life expectancy, infant mortality and access to electricity
explanation: The HDI, published by the UNDP, combines three equally weighted dimensions, health measured by life expectancy, education through mean and expected years of schooling, and a measure of income.

q: The Multidimensional Poverty Index is published jointly by
options: UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative
The ILO and the ILO
NITI Aayog and the Reserve Bank of India
The World Bank and the IMF
explanation: The global MPI is produced by the UNDP with the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, while NITI Aayog publishes a separate domestic index built on health, education and living standard indicators.

q: According to the Tendulkar Committee, the all-India poverty line should be
options: The median per capita consumption expenditure of the country
The per capita expenditure of the bottom 20 percent of households
The average per capita consumption expenditure of the poorest states
The per capita consumption expenditure of the poorest 10 percent of the population
explanation: The Tendulkar Committee fixed a single all-India poverty line at the per capita consumption expenditure of the poorest 10 percent of the population, with state specific lines adjusted upward to that level.

q: The Rangarajan Committee differed from the Tendulkar Committee in that it
options: Recommended state specific poverty lines derived from each state's own expenditure distribution
Recommended a uniform poverty line for rural and urban areas
Rejected the use of consumption expenditure as the poverty measure
Recommended a food energy based normative calorie requirement
explanation: The Rangarajan Committee used separate state specific poverty lines derived from the distribution of consumption expenditure within each state, unlike the single all-India line recommended by Tendulkar.

q: Disguised unemployment refers to
options: Persons who have stopped seeking work and left the labour force
New entrants who have not yet obtained their first job
Workers engaged in an activity whose marginal contribution to output is negligible
Workers unemployed for a short period due to seasonal factors
explanation: Disguised unemployment exists where too many workers are engaged in an activity such as farming on small holdings so that removing some of them would not reduce output, a situation typical of Indian agriculture.

q: Under the ILO definition, a person is counted as unemployed when he is
options: Working fewer hours than the full time standard
Not in employment and not actively seeking work
Without work but available for work, regardless of whether he seeks it
Without work, available for work and actively seeking work
explanation: The International Labour Organization's usual status approach counts a person as unemployed if he has no work, is available for work and is actively seeking work, which is the basis of the Indian labour force surveys.

q: Seasonal unemployment is best described as
options: Unemployment arising from a mismatch between worker skills and available jobs
Unemployment that occurs when the demand for labour varies with the season
Unemployment that lasts for more than six months
Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a downturn
explanation: Seasonal unemployment arises because demand for labour changes with the season, as in agriculture, tourism and construction, and it is pronounced in countries with a large agricultural workforce.

q: Which of the following is a growth indicator that does not take into account the distribution of income?
options: Multidimensional Poverty Index
Gini coefficient
Per capita real gross domestic product
Human Development Index
explanation: GDP per capita is an average measure of output per head and is silent on how that output is distributed, whereas the HDI, MPI and Gini coefficient explicitly capture distribution and human development.

q: Inclusive growth is best described as
options: Growth that benefits all sections of society, especially the poor, so that inequality does not rise
Growth driven entirely by the export oriented sector
Growth accompanied by a fall in the participation rate of women
Growth concentrated in the most dynamic states of the country
explanation: Inclusive growth means that the benefits of growth are widely shared, that the poorest grow faster than the average and that inequality does not widen, a theme adopted in the Eleventh Five Year Plan.

q: The First Five Year Plan in India was mainly directed towards
options: The development of heavy and machine based industries
Agricultural development with an emphasis on food self sufficiency
Establishment of a sound monetary and credit policy
Rapid industrialisation through an import substitution model
explanation: The First Plan (1951-56) was centred on agricultural development, irrigation and the aim of achieving self sufficiency in foodgrains, with heavy industry receiving attention only in the Second Plan.

q: Which Five Year Plan had higher growth with inclusive growth and employment as its stated objective?
options: The Twelfth Five Year Plan of 2012-17
The Second Five Year Plan of 1956-61
The Seventh Five Year Plan of 1985-90
The Eleventh Five Year Plan of 2007-12
explanation: The Eleventh Plan set the twin goals of higher growth and inclusive growth with employment, and it was the first plan to be framed as a National Employment Plan and monitored through the Five Year Plan Advisory Council.

q: The Fifth Five Year Plan of 1974-79 is notable for
options: Setting an explicit target for reducing the poverty ratio and introducing the rolling plan
Prioritising the development of the electronics industry
Giving the highest priority to defence production
Rejecting the five year allocation of resources to development goals
explanation: The Fifth Plan introduced the concept of a rolling plan and set out a specific target for reducing the poverty ratio, marking a decisive shift in planning towards poverty alleviation.

q: NITI Aayog was constituted to
options: Allocate five year plan funds among the states
Regulate the prices of essential commodities across the country
Supervise the working of the Central Board of Direct Taxes
Replace the Planning Commission with a cooperative and holistic institution that promotes state participation in policy making
explanation: NITI Aayog, which replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, does not allocate plan funds but works as a think tank that fosters cooperative federalism and provides policy advice to the centre and the states.

q: The Make in India programme launched in 2014 primarily aimed at
options: Setting up special economic zones exclusively for information technology firms
Doubling the number of public sector enterprises
Improving the competitiveness of the manufacturing sector through ease of doing business and better infrastructure
Replacing the Planning Commission with a new body for state coordination
explanation: Make in India sought to make India a global manufacturing hub by improving the ease of doing business, upgrading infrastructure and attracting investment, with twenty sectors identified for focused attention.

q: Economic development, as distinct from economic growth, implies
options: An increase in the per capita output of the country
A widening of the range of goods available to the population together with an improvement in living standards
A steady rise in the rate of investment in the economy
A rise in the real gross domestic product of the economy
explanation: Growth is a quantitative increase in output whereas development is broader, combining growth with structural change, diversification of the economy and improvements in health, education and living standards.

q: Rationalisation of the Consumer Price Index in India resulted in
options: Combining rural and urban prices into a single series
Fixing the base year as 1986-87 for the combined series
Reducing the number of price quotations collected in every city
Splitting the CPI into eight subgroups for the combined rural and urban series
explanation: The 2011 rationalisation replaced the separate rural and urban series with a CPI Combined, divided into eight subgroups, with the base year for the new series fixed at 2012.

q: Scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and elasticity belong primarily to the study of
options: International economics
Microeconomics
Macroeconomics
Public finance
explanation: These are the core tools of microeconomics, which analyses individual decision makers, firms and markets, whereas macroeconomics deals with aggregates such as inflation, output and unemployment.

q: In a two period consumption model, a consumer will borrow when
options: The consumer wants to hold a larger money balance for transaction purposes
Current income exceeds current consumption and the consumer prefers to hold money idle
Current income is below desired consumption and the consumer expects future income to be higher
The interest rate is zero and the consumer faces a liquidity constraint
explanation: Intertemporal choice leads to borrowing when present income is insufficient relative to present desired consumption and future income is expected to rise, so repayment is possible from future earnings.

q: The law of one price states that
options: Identical goods traded across countries cost the same in each country once transport costs and trade barriers are excluded
The domestic price of a non traded good equals the price of its closest substitute
The price of a good in the domestic market must equal its price in every foreign market
Exchange rates between two currencies remain constant over time
explanation: The law of one price holds that arbitrage keeps prices of identical goods equal across countries, with any difference explained by transport costs, tariffs and other barriers to trade.

q: Which of the following is an example of a positive externality?
options: A factory discharging smoke into the atmosphere
A vehicle emitting carbon dioxide on a public road
A coal fired power plant generating electricity for sale
A firm's research and development spending that benefits other firms in the industry
explanation: A positive externality occurs when an action creates benefits for third parties, as with knowledge spillovers from research and development, leading to under production of such goods by the market.

q: Comparative advantage as formulated by Ricardo rests on
options: The exchange rate at which goods are traded between countries
Differences in the relative costs of producing goods across countries rather than on absolute cost levels
The absolute productivity of each country in every industry
The size of a country's defence expenditure
explanation: Ricardo showed that even a country with absolute cost disadvantages can gain from trade if it specialises relatively in goods that it produces at a lower opportunity cost, which is the basis of comparative advantage.

q: Public goods are characterised by
options: Non rivalrous consumption and non excludability, which give rise to the free rider problem
The ability of producers to keep non consumers out of the market
High rivalry in consumption and easy exclusion of non payers
Perfectly competitive supply by a large number of small producers
explanation: Because one person's consumption does not reduce availability to others and non payers cannot be excluded, public goods tend to be under provided by the market, which is why they are financed through taxation.

q: The market failure that arises when the benefits of an activity spill over to third parties is
options: The Coase theorem
The paradox of thrift
The presence of positive externalities, which leads to under consumption
The tragedy of the commons
explanation: Positive externalities mean that private producers do not capture the full social benefit of their activity, so output is below the socially efficient level and corrective measures such as subsidies may be needed.

q: The term gross in Gross Domestic Product implies that
options: Net factor income from abroad has been included in the computation
Depreciation of capital assets has not been deducted from the value of output
Only the value of final goods has been included in the computation
The value of intermediate goods has been excluded from the computation
explanation: Gross measures do not deduct consumption of fixed capital, so GDP overstates the net addition to the stock of wealth, which is why net domestic product is also published.

q: The concept of a sunk cost implies that
options: Variable costs that vary with the level of output
The minimum cost that a firm must bear in the short run
Costs that can be recovered if the firm abandons the project
Costs already incurred that cannot be recovered and should not influence future decisions
explanation: A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered whatever the decision taken, so rational decisions depend only on future marginal costs and benefits.

q: The 'factor cost' or basic price measure of national income excludes
options: Indirect taxes and subsidies
Consumption of fixed capital
Compensation of employees
Rent and interest paid to factors of production
explanation: At factor cost the net product of the economy is shown without the impact of indirect taxes and subsidies, which is why GDP at market prices equals GVA at basic prices plus net taxes on products.

q: In the Indian system of national accounts, National Income is measured as
options: Gross Domestic Product at factor cost
Net Domestic Product at market prices
Net National Income at factor cost, that is net value added within the country plus net factor income from abroad
Gross National Product at market prices
explanation: National income is the net factor income accruing to the residents of the country, so it is net value added at factor cost within the country adjusted for net factor income from abroad.

q: Value added by an industry is computed as
options: Its gross sales less the value of its exports
The total value of all goods and services produced by the industry
The value of its output minus the value of intermediate goods and services consumed in production
The sum of wages and salaries paid by the industry
explanation: Value added equals output minus intermediate consumption, and summing value added across all industries gives GDP while avoiding the double counting of intermediate goods.

q: In the national accounts, intermediate consumption refers to
options: The depreciation of machinery and equipment
Goods and services used up in the production of other goods and services
The gross fixed capital formation of enterprises
Final goods purchased by households
explanation: Intermediate consumption comprises goods and services that are fully used up in production, and it is deducted from gross value added to avoid counting them as part of final output.

q: The primary sector continues to account for a disproportionately high share of employment in India because
options: Indian agriculture is the most mechanised among the major economies
Manufacturing output in India is not counted in the national accounts
The services sector does not create jobs in the Indian economy
A large number of workers remain in low productivity informal and subsistence agriculture
explanation: Because agricultural productivity remains low and non farm jobs have not grown fast enough, a very large share of the workforce continues to depend on low wage, low productivity agriculture.

q: Gross capital formation in the national accounts refers to
options: Addition to the stock of physical assets, including changes in inventories, after allowing for depreciation
The total savings of the household sector
The total investment of the corporate sector alone
Investment made by the government in roads and hospitals
explanation: Gross capital formation is the gross addition to the stock of fixed assets plus the change in stocks of inventories, and gross fixed capital formation is the part that corresponds to investment.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of gross capital formation as defined in the national accounts?
options: Acquisition of machinery and equipment
Repayment of an outstanding bank loan
Construction of a new factory building
Changes in stocks of finished goods
explanation: Repayment of a loan is a financial transaction and involves no new physical asset, so it is excluded from capital formation; only additions to fixed assets and inventories are counted.

q: Gross Value Added by economic activity is used in the national accounts to
options: Show the distribution of national income among households
Measure the rate of inflation in the economy
Show the sectoral composition of GDP while avoiding double counting of intermediate inputs
Measure the level of unemployment in the country
explanation: Since value added strips out the intermediate inputs used by each industry, adding the value added of all industries gives GDP without double counting and also reveals the sectoral composition of output.

q: The problem of double counting in national accounting arises because
options: Intermediate goods used in production are counted again as part of the value of the final product
Goods are counted both at market prices and at factor cost
Some sectors report both gross and net values of output
Some goods are counted both as inputs and as final outputs
explanation: Adding the output of all industries would count the value of intermediate goods several times, which is why the value added approach is used to compute GDP.

q: The Gini coefficient is used to measure
options: The rate at which poverty is reduced over a period of time
The share of income going to the top ten percent of the population
The ratio of the richest district to the poorest district
Inequality in the distribution of income or consumption
explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from zero for perfect equality to one for perfect inequality and is used to compare the degree of inequality across societies and over time.

q: The Lorenz curve depicts
options: The cumulative share of income held by the cumulative percentage of the population arranged from poorest to richest
The relationship between price and quantity demanded of a good
The growth rate of the money supply over time
The relationship between savings and income in an economy
explanation: The Lorenz curve plots cumulative population share against cumulative income share, and the Gini coefficient is derived from the area between this curve and the line of perfect equality.

q: The poverty line recommended by the Tendulkar Committee is based on
options: A calorie norm of 2100 calories per person per day for urban areas
The per capita consumption expenditure of the poorest ten percent of the population
The median consumption expenditure of the population
The average consumption expenditure of the bottom thirty percent of households
explanation: The committee derived a single all-India line from the consumption expenditure of the poorest ten percent of the population and adjusted the state specific lines upward to that level.

q: The National Sample Survey is conducted by
options: The Reserve Bank of India
NITI Aayog
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
The Central Statistical Organisation of the erstwhile Planning Commission
explanation: The National Sample Survey Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation conducts the periodic labour force survey and other household surveys.

q: The Periodic Labour Force Survey in India is conducted by
options: The Labour Bureau of the Ministry of Employment
The Ministry of Rural Development
The Indian Statistical Institute
The National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
explanation: The PLFS is conducted by the National Statistical Office, which replaced the quinquennial employment surveys and reports unemployment rates quarterly with annual averages.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Base year for WPI : 2012
Base year for constant price GDP : 2004-05
Base year for CPI Combined : 2010-11
Base year for CPI Combined : 2012
explanation: The CPI Combined series uses 2012 as its base year, while the WPI series uses 2011-12 and constant price GDP also uses 2011-12, so the other pairs are wrong.

q: In the classification used in the national accounts, the primary sector comprises
options: Manufacturing, mining and utilities
Trade, transport, banking and real estate
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and mining
Public administration, defence and education services
explanation: The primary sector covers the extraction of natural resources, that is agriculture and allied activities, forestry and fishing along with mining and quarrying of minerals.

q: Which of the following activities is classified under the secondary sector?
options: Software services exported over the internet
Sugar milling and food processing
Fishing and animal husbandry
Financial intermediation
explanation: Sugar milling and food processing transform raw materials into finished goods and therefore belong to the secondary or industrial sector, whereas the other options are primary or tertiary activities.

q: Gross Value Added at basic prices for the services sector is
options: The value of output less intermediate consumption, with net taxes on products shown separately
Net factor income earned from abroad
The value of output after deducting consumption of fixed capital
The gross value of exports of services alone
explanation: GVA is a gross measure, so consumption of fixed capital is not deducted from it, and net taxes on products are shown separately before arriving at GDP at market prices.

q: Net national income at factor cost is the measure used in India to compute
options: The real effective exchange rate of the rupee
The fiscal deficit of the Union Budget
Per capita income and the incidence of poverty
The monetary deficit of the central government
explanation: Per capita net national income at factor cost is the standard measure of average income and is also the denominator used in computing poverty ratios from consumption data.

q: Which of the following statements about the estimation of GDP in India is correct?
options: India does not publish a constant price series for GDP
Estimates are compiled by combining administrative sources, surveys and the accounts of the central and state governments
GDP is computed exclusively from the national accounts of the central government
GDP estimates are compiled from a census of enterprises conducted every five years
explanation: Indian national accounts combine data from the Central and State government accounts, enterprise surveys, the Economic Census, the labour force survey and price data from the CPI and WPI series.

q: In India, the advance estimates of GDP are released
options: Twice a year, in May and December
Once a year, in February
Quarterly, along with the quarterly monetary policy statement
First with a provisional estimate for the first quarter of the financial year
explanation: The National Statistical Office brings out quarterly estimates with a First Advance Estimate in May accompanied by a Provisional Estimate for the first quarter, followed by later revisions through the year.

q: Economic growth in India is best measured by
options: Real gross domestic product at constant prices, and per head for per capita growth
Nominal GDP converted at the current exchange rate
The ratio of exports to GDP
The index of industrial production
explanation: Real GDP at constant prices removes price effects and measures volume growth, and dividing it by population gives the per capita growth that matters for living standards.

q: Per capita income cannot by itself serve as a measure of well being because
options: It is calculated at current prices
It is an average that ignores distribution as well as non economic aspects of welfare
It is based on gross rather than net flows of income
It is measured at factor cost only
explanation: Per capita income is a distribution neutral average and ignores inequality, unpaid work, leisure, environment and access to public services, which is why the HDI and MPI were developed.

q: The multidimensional poverty index used by NITI Aayog measures poverty through a composite of
options: Employment type and wage levels
Access to banking and digital payments
Income and consumption levels
Health, education and standard of living indicators
explanation: The NITI Aayog index uses twelve indicators grouped under health, education and standard of living, and is computed for districts to guide convergence of schemes.

q: The Sustainable Development Goals replaced which earlier global development framework?
options: The Millennium Development Goals
The Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol
The Washington Consensus and the Doha Round
The Rio Declaration and Agenda 21
explanation: The seventeen Sustainable Development Goals and their 169 targets adopted in 2015 replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals that ran from 2000 to 2015.

q: The Human Development Report is published annually by
options: The International Monetary Fund
The World Economic Forum
The United Nations Development Programme
The World Bank
explanation: The UNDP brings out the Human Development Report every year, which ranks countries on the HDI and related indices such as the IHDI, GDI and the planetary pressure adjusted HDI.

q: The Gender Development Index published in the Human Development Report measures
options: Differences between female and male human development across health, education and income dimensions
The ratio of women's wages to men's wages in the formal sector
The share of women in the labour force of a country
The overall gender gap in economic participation
explanation: The GDI compares the HDI achieved by women and men in the same country and highlights gaps in health, education and income rather than only labour market participation.

q: The Inequality adjusted Human Development Index differs from the ordinary HDI by
options: Using mean years of schooling in place of expected years of schooling
Using GNI per capita at purchasing power parity instead of market exchange rates
Including a measure of the carbon footprint of the country
Discounting each dimension of human development for inequality in its distribution
explanation: The IHDI adjusts the HDI for the inequality that prevails within each of the three dimensions, so a country with a high HDI but wide disparities may have a much lower IHDI.

q: The Plan of Action to Exit Poverty in India is based on the idea that
options: Assets of the poor should be pooled into common property resources
Financial inclusion alone can lift every household out of poverty
A convergence approach covering health, nutrition, agriculture, water, sanitation, skilling, housing, education and social security can lift households above the poverty line
Every poor household should be guaranteed wage employment under MGNREGA
explanation: The Plan of Action to Exit Poverty identifies nine essential elements and emphasises convergence of investments through social, financial and physical infrastructure to raise household incomes sustainably.

q: The three components of the PM-KUSUM scheme are
options: Cold chain support, warehouse modernisation and market yard development
Solar power plants of 500 kW to 2 MW capacity, solar pumps for farmers and solarisation of grid connected small power plants
Drip and sprinkler irrigation, rainwater harvesting and soil health cards
Crop insurance, Kisan Credit Cards and integration with e-NAM markets
explanation: PM-KUSUM has three components, namely solar power plants of 500 kW to 2 MW per unit, standalone solar pumps for farmers and solarisation of grid connected small power plants.

q: The SDG India Index published by NITI Aayog is
options: An index of the competitiveness of Indian exports
A composite index of the health performance of districts
A ranking of states on their economic performance
A measure of progress of states and union territories towards the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals, scored out of 100
explanation: The SDG India Index scores each state and union territory on its progress against the seventeen SDGs, using 100 indicators, with a categorical score from 0 to 100 for each goal.

q: Which of the following is a limitation of GDP as a measure of economic performance?
options: GDP is measured for a single year only
GDP ignores the value of imports
GDP does not capture income distribution, unpaid household work or environmental degradation
GDP is computed at current prices in India
explanation: GDP is an aggregate of market valued production and omits the distribution of income, unpaid work of women and the depletion of natural assets, so it must be read with complementary social and environmental indicators.

q: The sectoral approach to national income accounting in India involves
options: Breaking down output and income generation by economic activity such as agriculture, industry and services
Studying the savings behaviour of households
Analysing the distribution of income between rural and urban areas
Studying the foreign trade performance of the economy
explanation: The sectoral approach presents national income as a sum of value added by individual industries, which reveals the structure of the economy and the relative importance of each sector.

q: The unorganised sector in the Indian economy refers to
options: Only the companies listed on the stock exchanges
The part of the economy outside the organised sector, which is larger in terms of employment and output
The part of the economy owned by the central government
Enterprises owned by foreign investors
explanation: The unorganised sector comprises small and unregistered enterprises and self employed workers and remains the larger of the two sectors in terms of both output and employment in India.

q: Per capita income as published in official statistics is based on
options: Gross domestic product divided by the total population
Net national income at factor cost divided by the mid-year population
Total national income divided by the labour force
Gross value added by services divided by the total population
explanation: Per capita income is net national income at factor cost divided by the mid-year population, and because it is a net concept it is used to compute the poverty ratios from consumption data.

q: The three methods of estimating national income in India are
options: The balance of payments method, the budget method and the census method
The input output method, the monetary method and the demographic method
The production method, the income method and the expenditure method
The value added method, the sales method and the tax method
explanation: National income can be estimated from the production side by value added, from the income side by summing factor incomes, and from the expenditure side by final consumption, investment and net exports.

q: In the expenditure approach, GDP is measured as
options: The sum of all factor incomes earned in production
The sum of value added across all industries
Total output less depreciation
Final consumption expenditure plus gross capital formation plus net exports
explanation: The expenditure method adds up final consumption expenditure, gross capital formation and net exports, which must equal output by the national accounting identity.

q: Narrow money supply in India, designated M1, comprises
options: Currency with the public, demand deposits with the banking system and other deposits with the RBI
Currency with the public plus time deposits with the banking system
Currency with the public, total deposits of the banking sector and postal savings deposits
Total currency issued by the RBI plus total deposits of scheduled banks
explanation: M1, the narrow money aggregate, covers currency with the public, demand deposits of the banking system and other deposits of the public with the Reserve Bank of India.

q: Broad money supply in India, designated M3, includes
options: Currency with the public and the reserve deposits of the central bank
Narrow money plus time deposits with the banking system and post office savings deposits
Currency with the public plus gold and silver held by households
Total currency issued by the RBI plus total deposits of scheduled commercial banks
explanation: M3 is the broad money aggregate and adds time deposits of the banking system and post office savings deposits to narrow money, capturing funds available for spending and investment.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional functions of money?
options: A measure of the physical size of the economy's output
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
explanation: The basic functions of money are medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value, with the basis of credit and the basis of payments to government taxes being additional functions, not a measure of output.

q: The currency deposit ratio in India indicates
options: The ratio of bank advances to total deposits
The proportion of a bank's net worth funded by reserves
The rate at which currency is converted into deposits
The extent of public preference for holding cash rather than bank deposits
explanation: The currency deposit ratio reflects how much of the system's funds the public prefers to hold as cash, and a rise in it signals a weakening of the money multiplier and of banks' capacity to create credit.

q: Basic savings deposit accounts with banks are included in the monetary aggregates as
options: M3, because they are maintained with post offices
M1, because they carry a minimum balance requirement
M1, because the RBI treats them as demand deposits
M2, because they carry interest
explanation: Basic savings deposit accounts are operable as demand accounts and the RBI includes them in the narrow money aggregate M1 along with current account balances.

q: Under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the minimum holding of paid up equity capital by the public in a banking company is
options: 50 per cent
51 per cent
75 per cent
26 per cent
explanation: Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act requires that at least 50 per cent of the paid up share capital of a banking company be held by the public, which is the condition for licensing a company as a bank.

q: The Cash Reserve Ratio is maintained by banks with
options: The State Governments
The Reserve Bank of India
The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
The Central Government
explanation: CRR is a proportion of net demand and time liabilities that banks must hold as cash or approved securities with the RBI, and the RBI does not pay interest on such balances.

q: Under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the Statutory Liquidity Ratio may be maintained in
options: Gold ornaments of customers held in bank lockers
Commercial paper and corporate bonds
Cash, gold or approved securities, mainly government securities
Equity shares of listed companies
explanation: SLR must be held in cash, gold or approved securities such as government bonds and treasury bills, and since these are government liabilities the central government provides a safe asset for this purpose.

q: A Non-Banking Financial Company is defined under
options: The Companies Act, 2013
The Finance Act
The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
explanation: Section 5A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, as amended in 1998, defines an NBFC as a company that can accept deposits from the public in any form and lend or invest in the assets specified by the RBI.

q: A non-banking financial company registered with the RBI cannot
options: Lend to individuals for consumption purposes
Issue commercial paper
Accept deposits from the public for a period of more than one year
Accept demand deposits from the public
explanation: An NBFC is not permitted to accept demand deposits from the public, because that would make it a bank, though it may accept time deposits and issue other instruments permitted by the RBI.

q: The Banking Ombudsman scheme for redressal of customer grievances operates under
options: The Reserve Bank of India
The Ministry of Finance
The Securities and Exchange Board of India
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority
explanation: The RBI administers the Banking Ombudsman scheme for retail banking complaints, and its earlier three separate schemes were merged into a single framework with a centralised complaint handling system.

q: Priority sector lending targets for commercial banks in India are determined by
options: The Securities and Exchange Board of India
The Government of India in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India
The RBI alone under the directions of the Monetary Policy Committee
The Finance Commission every five years
explanation: Priority sector lending norms are determined by the Government in consultation with the RBI and notified by the RBI, with the overall priority sector target fixed as a percentage of adjusted net bank credit.

q: Priority sectors for lending by commercial banks in India include
options: Only housing and education loans
Infrastructure and corporate lending to large companies
Agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewables and weaker sections
Only agriculture and export credit
explanation: The RBI's priority sector list covers agriculture and allied activities, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewables and credit to weaker sections, with sub-targets for each.

q: Under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, basic savings bank deposit accounts are provided with
options: A credit guarantee of Rs 5 lakh for each account holder
An interest rate of seven per cent fixed by the government
A mandatory life insurance cover of Rs 436 a year paid by the government
A RuPay debit card, an overdraft facility of up to Rs 10,000 after satisfactory operation and an accident insurance cover of Rs 2 lakh
explanation: Jan Dhan accounts come with a RuPay card, a zero balance overdraft of up to Rs 10,000 after six months and an accident insurance cover of Rs 2 lakh, and the overdraft scheme is now linked to the income of the account holder.

q: Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana provides loans to
options: Micro and small enterprises for income generating units in manufacturing, trading and services
Women entrepreneurs for setting up information technology parks
Large corporates for export diversification
Farmers for seasonal cropping needs
explanation: MUDRA lending is divided into Shishu, Kishore and Tarun categories for micro enterprises and small units in manufacturing, trading, services and allied activities, and the loan is collateral free.

q: The Unified Payments Interface allows
options: High value fund transfers in tranches of Rs 2 lakh and above
Instant person to merchant and person to person payments through an app or any other channel, round the clock
Only inter bank settlement through a central clearing house
Transfer of funds between two branches of the same bank
explanation: UPI is a real time retail payment system built on the Immediate Payment Service, and it enables small value transfers through mobile apps, bank apps, internet banking and other channels without any value ceiling.

q: Unlike the RTGS system, the National Electronic Funds Transfer operates on
options: A daily settlement cycle with no minimum transaction size
A fortnightly cycle for government transactions
A half hourly batch cycle with a minimum transaction size of Rs 2,000
A continuous real time basis with a minimum size of Rs 2 lakh
explanation: NEFT settles on a half hourly basis and allows any amount, while RTGS is a large value system operating in real time with a minimum transaction size of Rs 2 lakh.

q: The National Automated Clearing House is used primarily for
options: Settlement of stock market trades
High value inter bank fund transfers
Bulk processing of recurring credit and debit entries such as salary, dividend and interest payments
Real time mobile payments between individuals
explanation: NACH handles bulk electronic clearing of recurring collections and payments such as salaries, pensions, dividends, insurance premiums and utility dues under the eNACH framework.

q: The Immediate Payment Service was introduced in India in
explanation: IMPS was launched by the National Payments Corporation of India in November 2010 and enabled round the clock inter bank fund transfer and, later, person to person payments through the UPI platform.

q: A loan account is classified as a Non Performing Asset by the RBI when
options: It is being serviced through the help of a collection agent
It remains overdue beyond the stipulated period, such as 90 days for term loans
It has been restructured by the bank
It has been classified as a sub standard asset
explanation: An account becomes an NPA if the dues are not paid for more than 90 days for term loans and over 120 days for other demand loans and cash credit, the latter being termed as a non performing asset in the books of the bank.

q: Under the RBI's asset classification norms, sub standard assets are those that
options: Have lost the certainty of realisation and are treated as loss assets
Are being managed through the help of collection agencies
Are doubtful but have not yet been written off
Have remained non performing assets for a period of up to twelve months
explanation: Sub standard assets are NPAs of up to twelve months, doubtful assets have remained NPAs for more than twelve months, and loss assets are those where the loss has been identified but not yet written off.

q: The Capital Adequacy Ratio of a bank is computed as
options: Total assets divided by total deposits
Capital, both Tier 1 and Tier 2, expressed as a percentage of total risk weighted assets
Net profit after tax divided by total assets
Total capital employed divided by total borrowings
explanation: The CAR compares a bank's capital base with its risk weighted assets, so that the higher the risk of the assets the more capital the bank must hold, as required under the Basel norms.

q: Under the Basel norms, Tier 2 capital of a bank includes
options: The deposits of the public
Paid up equity share capital and reserves
Funds from the profits of the bank not distributed as dividend
Undisclosed reserves, revaluation reserves and certain subordinated debt instruments
explanation: Tier 1 comprises common equity and additional Tier 1 instruments, while Tier 2 includes undisclosed reserves, revaluation reserves, loan loss provisions and subordinated debt with a maturity of at least five years.

q: The Financial Stability and Development Council is chaired by
options: The Union Finance Minister
The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
The Chairman of the Finance Commission
The Chief Minister of the largest state
explanation: The FSDC, established in 2010, is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes the RBI Governor and the chairs of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and the Finance Commission as members.

q: Digital public infrastructure in India refers to
options: A framework for the mandatory digitisation of all small businesses
The information technology infrastructure provided to government schools
A shared digital layer of identity, payments and data such as Aadhaar, UPI linked banking and the account aggregator, built to deliver public services at scale
The collection of all government data in a single centralised database
explanation: Digital public infrastructure builds on the principle of open and interoperable digital public goods, of which Aadhaar, UPI and the account aggregator framework are the best known Indian examples.

q: The Account Aggregator framework in India enables
options: A fintech to obtain, with the consent of the customer, financial information from various banks for a specified purpose
The government to debit taxes directly from any bank account of a citizen
Banks to share loan application data without the consent of the customer
The RBI to collect the balances of all bank accounts in the country
explanation: The Account Aggregator is a consented, customer driven data sharing platform through which a fintech can pull financial information from the banks of a customer for a specified purpose, with no blanket access to bank data.

q: In the standard textbook classification, near money includes
options: Demand deposits with banks
Time deposits with banks and post office savings deposits, which can be readily converted into money
Gold and silver ornaments held by households
Currency notes held by the public
explanation: Assets that are not money in the strict sense but can be readily converted into money without much loss, such as savings and time deposits, are called near money and are part of the broader monetary aggregates.

q: Repo transactions are undertaken by the RBI with
options: The general public against government securities
Only non banking financial companies against corporate bonds
Commercial banks and other financial institutions against government securities
The Central Government against tax arrears
explanation: Under the repo, the RBI lends to banks against government securities with an agreement to repurchase them, thereby injecting liquidity into the system at the repo rate.

q: In a reverse repo transaction, the RBI
options: Lends directly to the Central Government
Raises the cash reserve ratio of banks
Lends to banks against securities with an obligation to repurchase
Borrows from banks by buying securities with an agreement to sell them back
explanation: In a reverse repo the RBI purchases securities from banks with an agreement to sell them back, which absorbs liquidity from the banking system at the reverse repo rate.

q: The Marginal Standing Facility allows banks to
options: Borrow for a period of up to one year against government securities
Borrow overnight from the RBI by dipping up to five per cent below the repo rate
Borrow overnight against corporate bonds
Borrow from the National Securities Depository
explanation: The MSF is a standing overnight liquidity facility under which banks can borrow from the RBI by dipping into their cash reserve tranche up to five per cent below the repo rate, and the MSF rate stands above the repo rate.

q: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility of the RBI provides overnight liquidity to banks against
options: Foreign currency deposits
Equity shares of listed companies
Government securities
Corporate bonds
explanation: Under the LAF, banks can borrow overnight from the RBI against government securities, with the RBI auctioning such liquidity through repo and reverse repo operations.

q: Which of the following is a quantitative instrument of monetary policy?
options: Repo rate
Margin requirements for lending against securities
Priority sector lending targets
Ban on fresh credit to certain sectors
explanation: Quantitative instruments influence the overall volume and cost of credit, such as the repo rate and the cash reserve ratio, while qualitative or selective instruments direct credit to particular sectors.

q: A bank's balance sheet is best described in terms of
options: The number of branches opened during the year
The total deposits mobilised from the public
Its income statement alone
Assets on one side and liabilities plus owners equity on the other
explanation: A balance sheet is a statement of financial position showing assets on one side and liabilities and capital on the other, and the difference between assets and liabilities gives the net worth of the bank.

q: The Financial Inclusion Index parameters used by the RBI include
options: The average size of bank balance sheets
The share of bank branches and ATMs located in villages
The number of listed companies on the stock exchanges
Account ownership, deposits and credit relative to GDP, and the number of outlets per 100,000 adults in rural areas
explanation: The Network for Financial Inclusion index measures account ownership, the share of deposits and credit in GDP and the number of outlets per 100,000 adults, and it underpins the monitoring of financial inclusion targets.

q: Credit Information Companies in India are registered with
options: The Reserve Bank of India
SEBI
IRDAI
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
explanation: Credit information companies, which compile credit records on borrowers for lenders, are registered and regulated by the RBI under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005.

q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code came into force in India on
options: 28 November 2015
1 April 2016
1 December 2016
1 January 2016
explanation: The IBC, 2016 received assent in May 2016 and came into force on 1 December 2016, creating a time bound corporate insolvency resolution process and establishing the NCLT and IBBI.

q: Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the corporate insolvency resolution process is to be completed within
options: 180 days from the date of admission
330 days from the date of admission, which may be extended by 90 days
270 days with no provision for extension
One year from the date of admission
explanation: The Code provides 330 days from the date of admission, including the 180 day moratorium, and the adjudicating authority may extend the period by 90 days where there is genuine difficulty in completing the process.

q: The moratorium period under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code refers to
options: The period for appeals against an approved resolution plan
The period during which no suit or proceeding can be instituted or continued against the corporate debtor, generally for 180 days
The period for which the Financial Creditors Committee remains constituted after approval of the plan
The period during which the liquidation process is carried out
explanation: Once a company is admitted to the resolution process, a moratorium of 180 days is declared during which no proceedings can be initiated or continued against the corporate debtor or its assets.

q: The National Company Law Tribunal is the adjudicating authority for
options: Tax disputes between the central and state governments
Consumer disputes relating to deficiency in services
Monetary policy decisions of the Reserve Bank of India
Insolvency resolution and liquidation proceedings of companies
explanation: The NCLT has jurisdiction over the corporate insolvency resolution process and liquidation of companies and their partners, while the NCLAT hears appeals against its orders.

q: The SARFAESI Act deals with
options: Enforcement of security interest in case of default by the borrower without the intervention of the court
Regulation of the securities market and stock exchanges
Prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing
Regulation of payment and settlement systems
explanation: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 allows secured creditors to enforce security without waiting for the delay of civil proceedings, subject to the borrower being given notice.

q: The regulatory authority for the insurance sector in India is
options: NABARD
SEBI
IRDAI
PFRDA
explanation: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India regulates insurers, while PFRDA supervises pension funds and NABARD is the apex institution for rural and agricultural credit.

q: Inflation in an economy is best described as
options: A one time rise in the price of a single commodity
A fall in the general price level over a quarter
A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services over a period of time
A rise in the price of traded goods only, without affecting domestic prices
explanation: Inflation is a sustained and generalised rise in the price level, whereas a one time increase in the price of a single commodity is a relative price change.

q: Demand-pull inflation arises when
options: The government reduces subsidies on key inputs
Aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's capacity to produce, pulling up prices
The cost of imported raw materials rises sharply
The exchange rate of the rupee appreciates sharply
explanation: Demand-pull inflation arises when spending outruns the capacity of the economy to supply goods and services, so firms respond by raising prices.

q: Cost-push inflation is best illustrated by
options: A sharp rise in international crude oil prices feeding into domestic fuel prices
A boom in consumer demand during a period of full employment
An increase in money supply without a matching growth in output
A large fiscal deficit financed by the printing of new notes
explanation: Cost-push inflation originates on the supply side when production costs rise, as with a crude oil price shock, and firms pass the higher costs on to consumers.

q: Built-in inflation refers to
options: Inflation caused by excess demand in the economy
Inflation caused by the government hiking administered prices
Inflation caused by a sharp rise in the international price of crude oil
Inflation generated by a wage price spiral as workers seek higher wages to match rising prices
explanation: Built-in inflation is inherent in the system when higher prices lead workers to demand higher wages, which raise costs again and perpetuate the price rise, so it is hard to control.

q: Which of the following would be most effective in controlling demand-pull inflation?
options: A cut in the corporate tax rate to boost investment
A large scale release of food stocks from the buffer
A reduction of import duties on essential commodities
A contractionary monetary policy involving higher interest rates and reduced liquidity
explanation: Demand-pull inflation is best checked by withdrawing demand through tighter monetary policy, while the other options are supply side or expansionary measures.

q: The Wholesale Price Index in India is released by
options: The National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics
The Central Board of Direct Taxes
The Office of the Economic Adviser under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
The Reserve Bank of India
explanation: The Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade compiles and releases the WPI, while the CPI is compiled by the National Statistical Office.

q: The Consumer Price Index Combined in India covers
options: Both rural and urban households across the country
Only rural households
Only urban households
Wholesale prices of traded goods
explanation: The CPI Combined, introduced with the 2011 rationalisation, is a single series covering both rural and urban households and is the metric used for inflation targeting.

q: Which of the following is a limitation of using the Consumer Price Index as a measure of inflation in India?
options: It is based on too few price quotations collected every year
It does not capture changes in asset prices such as house prices and share prices
It is computed for both rural and urban sectors
It is revised periodically to remove price biases
explanation: The CPI measures the prices of consumption goods and services and excludes asset transactions, so movements in house prices or share prices do not enter the index.

q: Headline inflation in India is measured by
options: The GDP deflator
The Wholesale Price Index
The Index of Industrial Production
The Consumer Price Index Combined
explanation: Headline inflation is the year on year change in the CPI Combined, which includes food and fuel and therefore reflects what households actually pay.

q: Core inflation in India is commonly measured as
options: The inflation in the price of non food manufactured goods only
The inflation measured by the GDP deflator
Consumer price inflation excluding the food and fuel components
Wholesale price inflation minus the price of crude oil
explanation: Core inflation strips out the volatile food and fuel components from the CPI, giving a better indication of the underlying trend in inflation.

q: The base year currently used for the Consumer Price Index Combined series is
explanation: The revised CPI series with eight subgroups uses 2012 as its base year, while the constant price GDP series and the WPI series use 2011-12.

q: The base year used for the compilation of the Wholesale Price Index in India is
explanation: The WPI series was rebased to 2011-12, so it uses the prices of that year as the base for measuring changes in wholesale prices.

q: Under the inflation targeting framework, the inflation target set by the Government in consultation with the RBI is
options: 5 per cent of the Wholesale Price Index with a band of 2 to 8 per cent
6 per cent of the GDP deflator with an upper tolerance of 8 per cent
4 per cent of the Consumer Price Index Combined with a band of 2 to 6 per cent
3 per cent of the CPI with a lower tolerance of 1 per cent
explanation: The Central Government fixes the inflation target at 4 per cent of the CPI Combined with an upper tolerance of 6 per cent and a lower tolerance of 2 per cent, in consultation with the RBI.

q: The Monetary Policy Committee of the Reserve Bank of India consists of
options: Six members, three from the RBI including the Governor who chairs it and three appointed by the Central Government, with two Union officials attending without voting rights
Five members, all drawn from the Reserve Bank of India
Seven members appointed entirely by Parliament
Six members appointed by the State Governments in proportion to their representation
explanation: The MPC has six members, three from the RBI including the Governor as Chairperson and three external members appointed by the Centre, while the Chief Financial Adviser and a Ministry of Finance representative attend without voting rights.

q: The mandate of the Monetary Policy Committee is to
options: Manage the foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate of the rupee
Maintain price stability in the country by keeping inflation within the target band
Regulate the licensing of banks and non banking financial companies
Set the tax rates and revenue expenditure of the central government
explanation: Section 45ZB of the amended RBI Act requires the MPC to determine the policy rate needed to achieve the inflation target, so price stability is its central mandate.

q: The inflation target in India is notified by
options: The Monetary Policy Committee of the RBI
The Ministry of Finance alone
The Reserve Bank of India alone under its own regulations
The Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India
explanation: Under Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, the Central Government determines the inflation target in consultation with the RBI and notifies it, and a failure to meet the target must be reported by the RBI to the Centre.

q: A situation in which prices rise while output growth stagnates or falls is called
options: Stagflation
Reflation
Deflation
Disinflation
explanation: Stagflation combines rising prices with stagnant or falling output and high unemployment, and it is particularly difficult to tackle with conventional monetary policy.

q: The Phillips curve depicts the relationship between
options: The rate of money supply growth and the rate of economic growth
The rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment
The exchange rate and the trade balance
The fiscal deficit and the current account deficit
explanation: The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment, suggesting that accepting higher inflation may reduce unemployment.

q: Food inflation in India carries a large weight in the CPI because
options: Food prices are excluded from the WPI but heavily weighted in the CPI
The government fixes most food prices in the administered price basket
Food items have a relatively high weight in the CPI basket and their prices are highly volatile
The CPI is computed exclusively on food and fuel items
explanation: Food has a high weight in the Indian CPI basket and is strongly influenced by harvests, weather and international prices, so food inflation moves headline inflation sharply.

q: Administered prices in India are
options: Fixed annually in the Union Budget without reference to market conditions
Determined by an international body such as the World Bank
Fixed by the Reserve Bank of India through its monetary operations
Announced periodically by the government for crops such as sugarcane and paddy and for items such as fertilisers, petrol and LPG
explanation: Administered prices are announced by the government at the beginning of the season or the year for crops such as sugarcane and paddy and for petroleum products, fertilisers and LPG.

q: The fertiliser subsidy in India is
options: Paid to farmers directly in cash for every bag of fertiliser bought
Discontinued entirely since the introduction of the nutrient based subsidy scheme
Granted only for urea produced from domestic gas and never for demeritised phosphate
Provided mainly to fertiliser producers, who in turn sell subsidised fertiliser to farmers below the cost
explanation: The nutrient based subsidy is paid to manufacturers who sell fertiliser to farmers at subsidised prices, with the subsidy notified per kilogram of nutrients for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

q: The fuel subsidy in India
options: Is paid to oil marketing companies to fully compensate them for taxes on crude oil
Was progressively reduced to nil on petrol and diesel by 2020-21, with subsidised LPG and kerosene retained
Is paid directly to consumers of petrol and diesel at the pump
Has been in place continuously since 2014 without any change
explanation: The government phased out the subsidy on petrol and diesel, taking it to nil by 2020-21, while retaining subsidies on domestic LPG and kerosene for the poorer households.

q: The repo rate affects the general price level of the economy through
options: A direct change in the administered prices of fertilisers and fuel
A change in the base year of the price index used to measure inflation
The cost of borrowing for banks and the resulting effect on credit demand and aggregate demand
The statutory limits on cash withdrawals by the public
explanation: A change in the repo rate changes the cost of bank borrowing, which passes on to lending rates, credit demand and aggregate demand, and eventually to prices and output.

q: The main instrument used by the RBI to absorb excess liquidity from the banking system is
options: Sale of government securities under open market operations
Reduction in the cash reserve ratio
Reduction in the repo rate
Purchase of foreign currency from authorised dealers
explanation: Selling securities in the open market drains rupees from the banking system, and the reverse repo is the other such instrument used to absorb liquidity.

q: Core inflation is useful for monetary policy because
options: It is computed from wholesale prices of manufactured goods only
It excludes volatile food and fuel prices and so gives a better signal of underlying inflationary pressure
It reflects the impact of supply disruptions on food prices
It is the only measure on which the RBI may base its policy rate
explanation: Since food and fuel prices are volatile and subject to supply shocks, core inflation gives the MPC a clearer signal of the persistent component of price pressure.

q: The inflation targeting framework in India was made operational with effect from
options: January 2016
April 2014
April 2012
April 2016
explanation: The Finance Act, 2016 amended the RBI Act to create a statutory Monetary Policy Committee and the flexible inflation targeting framework was put in place from 1 April 2016.

q: Which of the following is a supply side measure to curb inflation?
options: Increasing the buffer stocks of foodgrains and augmenting their release through fair price shops
Restricting the supply of consumer credit through the RBI
Raising the repo rate to tighten liquidity
Lowering the statutory liquidity ratio
explanation: Buffer stocks and targeted distribution of foodgrains raise availability and moderate food prices, whereas the other options are demand side monetary measures.

q: The index of food inflation in India is compiled and released by
options: The Central Board of Direct Taxes
The Department of Consumer Affairs
The National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
The Reserve Bank of India
explanation: Food inflation is a component of the CPI released by the National Statistical Office, which also publishes the food price index for monitoring supply conditions.

q: When the RBI raises the repo rate, the most likely first order effect is
options: It raises the cost of borrowing, dampening credit demand and moderating inflationary pressure over time
An immediate fall in food prices
A rise in the price of petroleum products
A rise in the price of government securities and hence the cost of borrowing for the government
explanation: Higher repo rates raise the cost of bank funds, which passes on to lending rates and credit demand, so aggregate demand and inflation are dampened with a time lag.

q: The base effect in the measurement of inflation means that
options: The base year of the index is changed every five years
The price index is calculated using the average prices of a base period
A high inflation rate in the current year may appear lower because the comparison is with a base year that had unusually high prices
Inflation is measured after adjusting for the purchasing power of the base year
explanation: Inflation is measured against the price level of a year earlier, so an unusually high base year can make the current rate look deceptively low even when prices are still rising.

q: Which of the following is a correct match?
options: Consumer Price Index: compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser
Repo rate: fixed by the Government of India
Monetary Policy Committee: constituted under the Companies Act
Inflation target in India: 4 per cent with a band of plus or minus 2 percentage points
explanation: The inflation target is 4 per cent with a tolerance band of 2 to 6 per cent, the repo rate is set by the MPC, the MPC is a statutory body under the RBI Act, and the CPI is compiled by the NSO.

q: The weighted median inflation measure used by the RBI is computed as
options: The inflation rate obtained by dividing the food index by the non food index
The inflation rate of the median state in terms of CPI, weighted by the shares of states in the CPI
The simple average of the inflation rates of all states and union territories
The average of the inflation rates of the ten largest states by GDP
explanation: The weighted median inflation takes the state whose CPI weight is the median and reports its inflation rate, so it is less distorted by large states than a simple average.

q: The implicit weighted median inflation is published by
options: NITI Aayog
The Reserve Bank of India
The Central Statistical Organisation
The Office of the Economic Adviser
explanation: The RBI publishes the implicit weighted median inflation as a measure of underlying inflation pressure for use in monetary policy analysis.

q: Printing currency notes to finance a large fiscal deficit is described as
options: Demand pull inflation
Stagflation
Cost push inflation
Monetisation of the fiscal deficit
explanation: When the government meets its financing needs by issuing currency, it adds to the money supply without any matching output, creating monetary overhang and inflationary pressure.

q: Which measure can help check inflation arising from a depreciation of the rupee?
options: A rise in the fiscal deficit of the central government
An increase in the money supply of the economy
Sustained inflows of foreign exchange that add to the foreign exchange reserves
A sharp rise in the administered prices of fertilisers
explanation: A weaker rupee raises the domestic cost of imports such as crude oil, but inflows of foreign exchange enable the RBI to build reserves and smooth the adjustment.

q: The Phillips curve is considered an unreliable guide for policy because
options: The trade-off between inflation and unemployment is not stable over time and supply shocks can shift the curve
It is difficult to measure the rate of unemployment accurately
It can only be applied to the economies of developed countries
It measures inflation in terms of the GDP deflator only
explanation: Empirical estimates show the inflation unemployment trade-off shifting over time, and supply shocks can move the whole curve, so the Phillips curve is not a dependable policy rule.

q: The CPI Combined, and not the WPI, is used as the metric for monetary policy targeting because
options: The WPI is published only once a year
The WPI excludes services and cannot be computed for individual states
The WPI is compiled by the RBI and the CPI by the government
It captures the prices that consumers actually pay and includes services and housing rents
explanation: The CPI captures the household basket of consumption including services and rents, so it reflects the inflation experienced by consumers, which is what the MPC targets.

q: Real wages of an employee refer to
options: The nominal wages adjusted for the level of employment
The purchasing power of money wages, obtained by adjusting nominal wages for the prevailing inflation rate
The total wage income of the economy
The wages paid to all workers in the organised sector
explanation: Real wages measure what a worker's money wages can buy, so they fall when prices rise faster than nominal wages, which is why wage negotiations are linked to the cost of living index.

q: The government raised excise duty on petrol and diesel in July 2021 mainly in order to
options: Fund the construction of highways through the cess collected
Reduce the losses of oil marketing companies caused by price freezes
Offset the revenue loss from the reduction in excise duty in 2020-21 rather than to raise additional resources
Compensate the states for their loss of sales tax revenue
explanation: The July 2021 increase in excise duty was described as a partial restoration of the revenue lost when duties were cut in March 2020, rather than as a fresh revenue mobilisation measure.

q: Inflation targeting in India aims primarily at
options: Achieving and maintaining price stability, understood as a stable and moderate rate of inflation over the medium term
Keeping the exchange rate of the rupee stable against the dollar
Ensuring that food prices remain stable irrespective of harvest conditions
Reducing the fiscal deficit of the central government to 3 per cent of GDP
explanation: Price stability in the sense of a moderate and predictable inflation rate is the primary goal of inflation targeting, with growth and employment considered as secondary objectives.

q: The budget deficit shown in the Annual Financial Statement equals
options: The revenue deficit
The primary deficit
The fiscal deficit minus interest payments
Total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowings
explanation: The budget deficit is total expenditure less total receipts including borrowings, and it is smaller than the fiscal deficit by the amount of net market borrowing taken by the government.

q: Which of the following pairs regarding budget terminology is correctly matched?
options: Revenue deficit: revenue expenditure less revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit: total expenditure less total receipts including borrowings
Primary deficit: fiscal deficit plus interest payments
Budget deficit: revenue deficit less capital expenditure
explanation: The revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, while the other three pairs invert or distort the correct relationships between the four deficit measures.

q: Fiscal policy refers to
options: The regulation of the volume of money supply in the economy
The government's policy regarding public spending, taxation and borrowing to influence aggregate demand and the economy
The central bank's policy of regulating interest rates and credit
The government's policy on the exchange rate and foreign trade
explanation: Fiscal policy covers taxation, public expenditure and government borrowing, all of which the government uses to influence aggregate demand, employment and the level of prices.

q: The instruments of fiscal policy include
options: Repo rate and the reverse repo rate
Cash reserve ratio and open market operations
Taxation, public expenditure and government borrowing
The money multiplier and the velocity of money
explanation: Taxation, public expenditure and borrowing are the fiscal instruments, whereas interest rates, reserve ratios and open market operations belong to monetary policy.

q: The Laffer curve depicts
options: The relationship between unemployment and inflation
The relationship between the tax rate and tax revenue, which rises up to a point and then falls
The relationship between the money supply and the price level
The relationship between the exchange rate and the trade balance
explanation: The Laffer curve shows that tax revenue rises with the tax rate up to a point and then falls as very high rates discourage work, investment and tax compliance.

q: According to the Laffer curve, tax revenue falls when the tax rate becomes so high that
